teaser.text: Fortis owns utilities that deliver electricity and gas through high-voltage lines, local wires and pipelines. It earns mainly by charging for access to those networks, while some businesses also generate, buy or sell the energy moving through them.

blocks.heading: Where could Fortis's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted path reaches C$76.97 in October 2027 and C$79.97 in October 2028. It reaches C$84.15 in October 2029, a 19% total return with dividends. The last-date range is C$57.47 to C$114.49. Today's price is C$77.52.

The bull case requires timely TEP recovery, firm large-load demand and on-schedule ITC construction. It reaches C$114.49 by October 2029 from C$90.91 in October 2027. Its probability is 20% because prospective demand remains conditional and some ITC projects are not yet under construction. The base case receives 55%: it requires plan delivery, not flawless execution, and is supported by regulated investment, analyst expectations and the dividend record.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Fortis?

paragraphs.text: The C$28.8 billion capital plan targets 7% annual rate-base growth, supporting the base path. The bear row reaches only C$2,084 million because rate lag, affordability limits, project delays and financing costs persist. The bull row reaches C$2,516 million because TEP recovery and ITC investment convert into earnings faster. TEP's rate decision is scheduled for November 17, 2026, making it a dated catalyst.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Fortis really make?

paragraphs.text: Capital spending is different because Fortis must pay contractors to build or renew networks. The result is negative free cash flow before dividends. Fortis also shows a stricter “real” free-cash-flow view by treating stock compensation as an economic cost. Interest paid is already reflected in operating cash, so subtracting it again would count the same outflow twice.

blocks.heading: How much does Fortis pay its shareholders?

paragraphs.text: Revenue grew 5.8% in 2025 while operating margin was 28.7%; pass-through sales can rise without equal profit growth. Net debt rose from C$25,788 million in 2021 to C$34,267 million in 2025. The company’s own free cash flow was negative in 2021 and 2022. Dividends per share rose from C$2.08 in 2021 to C$2.51 in 2025. Diluted EPS rose from C$2.61 in 2021 to C$3.40 in 2025 as average diluted shares grew each year. Shares trade at 22.7x trailing P/E and 20.0x next-12-month P/E. The dividend yield is 3.3%, against a 0.0% buyback yield.

blocks.heading: Is Fortis’s dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: Free cash flow is the cash left after operating cash flow pays for capital spending. Fortis’s free cash flow was negative in 2021 and 2022, so operations alone did not fund both construction and shareholder distributions. Fortis therefore relied on borrowing, asset sales and shareholder capital. That does not prove the projects were poor; it means their cash returns arrived later than their construction bills.

Dividends added to the financing pressure. A dividend-reinvestment plan lets shareholders use dividends to buy new Fortis shares instead of taking cash. Fortis says its plan offers a 2% discount, so participating shareholders help keep money inside the company while increasing the number of shares that will share future profits. Buybacks were zero in every year, which meant Fortis did not use cash to reduce its share count.

paragraphs.text: Management’s C$28.8 billion 2026–2030 capital plan targets 7% annual rate-base growth. It targets 4%–6% annual dividend growth through 2030. Disposed businesses are expected to reduce 2026 EPS by C$0.05.

Dividends begin at C$2.62 after a 4.4% increase from the latest C$2.51 annual payment. The base path reaches C$2.89 by October 2029, close to management's 4%–6% target. The bear case freezes the dividend after the first increase, while the bull reaches C$2.96 by applying the top of guidance as recovery improves. The five-year record shows increases every year, which supports growth but not an unlimited payout.

blocks.heading: Has Fortis kept its past promises?

paragraphs.text: Fortis’s fourth-quarter dividend rose 4.1% in 2025, continuing 52 years of increases in dividends paid. Management reaffirmed 4–6% annual growth through 2030, but the missed cash-flow target shows that delivery was uneven. The fairest conclusion is therefore mixed: Fortis’s leaders have experience, exposure and a record of delivery, but shareholders still need to test how independently the board challenges them and how honestly performance is measured.

blocks.heading: What is Fortis's recent results trend?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash rose sharply, yet capital spending remained higher. Tax-credit sales and payment timing strengthened the quarter, so the cash increase should not be projected mechanically. Across eight quarters, Canadian heating and Arizona cooling create visible seasonality. The right test is year-on-year and year-to-date growth followed by a regulatory check.

blocks.heading: What should Fortis watchers look for next?

paragraphs.text: Fortis will report third-quarter results and a new five-year capital outlook on November 3, 2026. The useful comparison is project by project: which costs more, which enters service later and which needs more equity. A larger spending total can hide slower delivery.

Tucson Electric Power’s rate case is scheduled for a decision by November 17, 2026. It seeks an approximately 13% increase in annual revenue and more regular formula adjustments. The unresolved challenge to Arizona’s formula-rate authority could determine how long rising costs remain outside customer bills.
